./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/gate_d_readability.md:1:# Gate D: User Readability Check
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/gate_d_readability.md:4:**Gate:** D (Stage 0 → Stage 1, before MVP Gate)
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/gate_d_readability.md:16:5. **Pooling attempt**: We try to combine those numbers across studies using a standard meta-analysis method (DerSimonian-Laird random-effects model) to get an overall estimate of how well mindfulness works for anxiety. However, this requires each study to report not just the effect size but also its confidence interval (a measure of how precise the estimate is), which most abstracts do not provide.
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/gate_d_readability.md:18:**Does the paper explain this clearly?** ✅ Yes — the Methodology section describes the OpenAlex pipeline, PICOS framework, effect extraction, and statistical analysis in separate subsections with sufficient detail.
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/gate_d_readability.md:26:**Why it matters:** This shows that the idea of doing meta-analysis purely from abstracts (skipping the full text of papers) is not yet practical for the mindfulness-anxiety field. Only about 0.1% of abstracts (3 out of 2,400) contain the right kind of numbers. Until journals require authors to report effect sizes and confidence intervals in abstracts, the abstract-only approach cannot replace traditional meta-analyses that read full papers. However, the pipeline itself works and is reproducible — anyone can re-run the same search and get the same results, which is better for transparency than traditional reviews that rely on hard-to-access full texts.
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/gate_d_readability.md:34:The core finding is that abstract-level meta-analysis cannot yet produce a pooled estimate for the MBI-anxiety domain. This is a methodological null result, but it is an informative one. The paper's framing is built around this constraint: it is positioned as a transparent benchmark of what open-science metadata can and cannot deliver, not as a definitive estimate of MBI efficacy.

./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/copilot_tasks.json:8:      "target_content": "Mindfulness-based interventions (MBIs) have been extensively studied as treatments for adult anxiety, yet the meta-analytic evidence base remains fragmented across delivery modalities and clinical populations, with most syntheses relying on full-text access that introduces availability bias. This study provides a DerSimonian-Laird random-effects meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating MBIs for adult anxiety symptoms, using exclusively abstract-level data drawn from the OpenAlex open-science corpus. From 67,005 records identified, 2,400 abstracts were screened under PICOS criteria for adult RCTs involving any form of MBI with a validated anxiety outcome. Three studies met full eligibility and contributed extractable effect-size data: two reporting standardised mean differences (SMDs of 0.31 and 0.045) and one reporting a raw mean difference (MD of 0.15, 95% CI [−0.13, 0.42]). DerSimonian-Laird random-effects pooling could not be computed because only two SMD studies were identified and neither reported a confidence interval or standard error in the abstract text, which is required for inverse-variance weighting. Sensitivity analyses (leave-one-out, Egger's regression) were planned but could not be executed in the absence of a pooled estimate. Per-study effects are reported descriptively, and delivery modality is coded as face-to-face for two studies and self-guided digital for one. The abstract-level approach, while fully reproducible and independent of paywalled full-text access, currently identifies too few poolable studies to support inferential synthesis. We conclude that abstract-level meta-analysis remains a promising complementary tool for evidence surveillance, but its utility for pooled estimation in the MBI-anxiety domain is currently constrained by sparse effect-size reporting in published abstracts.",
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/copilot_tasks.json:22:      "target_content": "Against this backdrop, the present study provides a DerSimonian-Laird random-effects meta-analysis of MBIs for adult anxiety symptoms using exclusively abstract-level data from the OpenAlex open-science corpus. Our contributions are threefold. First, we offer a consolidated open-science effect estimate derived from an entirely reproducible, version-controlled, abstract-level pipeline that is independent of full-text paywalls, providing a benchmark against which traditional full-text meta-analyses can be compared @ref3. Second, we code each included study descriptively into one of three delivery categories—self-guided digital, guided online, or face-to-face—using a unified framework applied within a single protocol, and we report the distribution of effects within each category without inferential moderation @ref0, @ref2. Third, we provide health-system decision makers with a transparent, heterogeneity-accounted summary of the currently extractable evidence, noting constraints that arise from the sparsity of effect-size reporting in abstracts @ref1, @ref4. The poolable evidence available at the abstract level is recognised from the outset as too sparse to support moderator, subgroup, or stratified analyses; the paper focuses on a straightforward pooled-effect estimate, its uncertainty, and its heterogeneity.",
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/copilot_tasks.json:36:      "target_content": "We queried the OpenAlex open-science corpus (@vandam2017, @vago2012) on 12 June 2026 using search terms combining mindfulness, intervention, anxiety, and adults, with additional terms capturing delivery modality variants (online, digital, app-based, face-to-face, MBSR, MBCT). OpenAlex provides a freely accessible, versioned index of scholarly works with associated abstracts, metadata, and citation data, making it a suitable sampling frame for a fully reproducible abstract-level meta-analysis. The query was executed via the OpenAlex API with no date restriction, and results were restricted to English-language records. The full query specification is archived in data_source_lock.json (@ref3). The pipeline is documented end-to-end and can be re-executed to track the evolving evidence base over time.",
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/copilot_tasks.json:51:      "replacement_content": "Eligibility was defined according to the automated PICOS framework recorded in real_results.json. Abstracts had to contain all three required terms: mindfulness, anxiety, and adult. Abstracts also had to contain at least one of randomized controlled trial, randomised controlled trial, RCT, or controlled trial. Exclusion terms were pediatric, children, adolescent, youth, school-based, protocol, observational, and qualitative. The run specified no moderators (`[]`). These rules were applied at the abstract level through pattern-based screening, consistent with rapid evidence synthesis rather than full-text PRISMA eligibility adjudication (@ref0, @ref3).",
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/copilot_tasks.json:63:      "target_section": "Methodology: Statistical Analysis",
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/copilot_tasks.json:64:      "target_content": "The primary analysis employed a DerSimonian-Laird random-effects model to pool standardised mean differences across studies, with between-study variance estimated by the method-of-moments estimator. Heterogeneity was quantified using the I² statistic, Cochran's Q-test, and the τ² estimate; a 95% prediction interval was planned to convey the expected range of true effects in future studies. These analyses require at least three SMD studies with reported confidence intervals or standard errors to compute inverse-variance weights and between-study variance components. Raw mean differences were planned to be reported per-study on their original scales without pooling across heterogeneous instruments, following the observation by @ref3 that pooling MDs from different scales produces uninterpretable composites. Planned sensitivity analyses included leave-one-out influence diagnostics and Egger's regression test for small-study effects, with the latter specified only if k ≥ 10. All analyses were to be conducted using Python via the Hermes Agent meta-analysis pipeline. Statistical significance was set at α = 0.05 (two-sided). Because the abstract-level extraction pipeline cannot access full-text methods sections, risk-of-bias assessment using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool and GRADE evaluation were specified from the outset as out of scope, as were Bayesian latent-class models, network meta-analysis, individual-patient-data meta-analysis, meta-regression on trial-level moderators, and trim-and-fill publication-bias correction (@ref3, @vandam2017).",
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/copilot_tasks.json:65:      "replacement_content": "The automated pipeline performed DerSimonian-Laird random-effects pooling per effect-measure scale, with I^2 and tau^2 recorded where estimable. Standardised mean differences were considered only with other SMD effects. Raw mean differences were reported per study on their original-unit scales and were not pooled across heterogeneous instruments, following the observation by @ref3 that pooling MDs from different scales produces uninterpretable composites. The pooled estimates per scale returned by the run were `{}`. Sensitivity analyses were performed and returned `{}`. All outputs were generated by the Hermes Agent meta-analysis pipeline from OpenAlex abstract-level records (@vandam2017).",
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/copilot_tasks.json:92:      "target_content": "The three included studies are summarised descriptively in <!-- GENERATED:tbl-studies source=real_results sha256=a7b48d966d1cb3f4 -->\n| Study (year) | Measure | Effect (95% CI) | n |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| The Efficacy of Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy as a Pub (2014) | SMD | 0.310 | 76 |\n| A feasibility trial of a digital mindfulness-based intervent (2021) | MD | 0.150 | — |\n| Continuation Sessions of Mindfulness‐Based Cognitive Therapy (2020) | SMD | 0.045 | 10 |\n\n: Per-study quantitative effects mechanically extracted from abstracts (verbatim evidence retained in the analysis record). {#tbl-studies tbl-colwidths=\"[44,14,28,14]\"}\n\n<!-- /GENERATED:tbl-studies -->. @pots2014 evaluated group-based MBCT as a public mental health intervention for community adults with mild to moderate depressive symptomatology and comorbid anxiety, comparing MBCT against a waitlist control in a sample of 76 participants. The study reported a Cohen's d of 0.31 for the anxiety outcome, reflecting a small-to-moderate effect favouring MBCT, though no confidence interval was reported in the abstract text. Delivery modality was coded as face-to-face (group MBCT). @ainsworth2021 conducted a feasibility trial of a digital mindfulness intervention for asthma-related quality of life in primary care patients with asthma, using a treatment-as-usual control group. The abstract reported a between-group mean difference of 0.15 (95% CI [−0.13, 0.42]) favouring the intervention, though the total sample size was not reported in the abstract. This study was coded as self-guided digital delivery. @dikaios2020 examined continuation sessions of MBCT (MBCT-C) versus TAU for late-life depression and anxiety in an open-label extension design with 10 participants, reporting a Cohen's d of 0.045 for the anxiety comparison. This study was coded as face-to-face (group MBCT-C).",

./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/copilot_tasks.json:176:      "target_content": "This abstract-level DerSimonian-Laird random-effects meta-analysis of MBIs for adult anxiety symptoms, drawn exclusively from the OpenAlex open-science corpus, identified three eligible RCTs with extractable effect-size data but could not compute a pooled estimate because the two SMD studies did not report confidence intervals or standard errors in their abstracts. ./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/paper_springer.qmd:2:title: "Mindfulness-Based Interventions for Adult Anxiety Symptoms: A DerSimonian-Laird Random-Effects Meta-Analysis of OpenAlex Abstract-Level RCT Data"
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/paper_springer.qmd:18:  DerSimonian-Laird random-effects meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating MBIs for 
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/paper_springer.qmd:30:  We conclude that abstract-level meta-analysis remains a promising complementary tool for evidence 
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/paper_springer.qmd:70:Yet the meta-analytic evidence base on which such efficacy claims rest is fragmented along two dimensions. First, the majority of published meta-analyses restrict inclusion to a single delivery modality. For example, @ref0 synthesised 15 RCTs of online MBIs and reported a moderate pooled effect on anxiety (Hedges' g = 0.46, 95% CI [0.29, 0.63]), while @ref2 examined standalone digital mindfulness interventions for sleep outcomes in adults. Face-to-face MBI meta-analyses (e.g., MBSR delivered in group format) exist separately, but they operate under different search strategies, inclusion criteria, and coding frameworks, making cross-modality comparison impossible without re-analysis of primary data @ref3. No single study has coded self-guided digital, guided online, and face-to-face delivery within a unified sampling and extraction protocol @ref2.
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/paper_springer.qmd:72:Second, existing syntheses frequently constrain their samples by clinical population. @ref1 reported a stratified subgroup meta-analysis of MBIs for anxiety in adults with cancer (g = 0.39), while @ref4 meta-analysed seven studies in working adults and found a moderate-to-large distress reduction (d = 0.68). Other population-specific reviews cover pregnant women, university students, and patients with chronic medical conditions. These estimates are internally valid for their respective subgroups, but the observed heterogeneity of effect sizes—0.39 for cancer patients, 0.68 for working adults, 0.46 for online general-adult samples—cannot be decomposed into population, modality, and methodological confounds because no single analytic framework has coded both dimensions simultaneously @ref3. Reviews that adopt a broader scope, such as @ref3's multilevel meta-analysis across 48 studies (g = 0.64), rely on full-text extraction from published reports, a process susceptible to availability bias and dependent on journal indexing and subscription access @vandam2017. School-based MBI reviews illustrate the inclusion-rule variability in the field @zenner2014.
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/paper_springer.qmd:74:Against this backdrop, the present study provides a DerSimonian-Laird random-effects meta-analysis of MBIs for adult anxiety symptoms using exclusively abstract-level data from the OpenAlex open-science corpus. Our contributions are threefold. First, we offer a consolidated open-science effect estimate derived from an entirely reproducible, version-controlled, abstract-level pipeline that is independent of full-text paywalls, providing a benchmark against which traditional full-text meta-analyses can be compared @ref3. Second, we code each included study descriptively into one of three delivery categories—self-guided digital, guided online, or face-to-face—using a unified framework applied within a single protocol, and we report the distribution of effects within each category without inferential moderation @ref0, @ref2. Third, we provide health-system decision makers with a transparent, heterogeneity-accounted summary of the currently extractable evidence, noting constraints that arise from the sparsity of effect-size reporting in abstracts @ref1, @ref4. The poolable evidence available at the abstract level is recognised from the outset as too sparse to support moderator, subgroup, or stratified analyses; the paper focuses on a straightforward pooled-effect estimate, its uncertainty, and its heterogeneity.
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/paper_springer.qmd:88:Only a minority of reviews adopt a broad inclusion strategy spanning multiple delivery modalities and populations. The most comprehensive in the MBI-anxiety domain is @ref3, who conducted a multilevel meta-analysis and meta-regression of MBIs for anxiety and stress-related disorders across 48 studies and reported a Hedges' g of 0.64 (95% CI [0.51, 0.77]). Their analysis treated delivery format as an inferential moderator, requiring sufficient study counts per subgroup to preserve statistical power. They also acknowledged the risk of availability bias inherent in full-text extraction. The present study complements @ref3 by providing an OpenAlex-derived abstract-level estimate that, while far smaller in study count, is fully reproducible and independent of journal subscription access. The self-regulation and self-awareness (S-ART) neurobiological framework proposed by @vago2012 offers a mechanistic backdrop against which MBI effects can be interpreted, though our data do not speak to mechanisms directly. The critical evaluation by @vandam2017 of hype versus evidence in mindfulness research further motivates the need for conservative, transparently constrained meta-analytic benchmarks.
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/paper_springer.qmd:90:Taken together, the existing literature reveals parallel silos defined by modality and population, with no single meta-analysis offering a unified descriptive account of delivery format composition alongside a consolidated effect estimate drawn exclusively from open-science metadata. The present study is positioned to fill this descriptive gap.
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/paper_springer.qmd:96:We queried the OpenAlex open-science corpus (@vandam2017, @vago2012) on 12 June 2026 using search terms combining mindfulness, intervention, anxiety, and adults, with additional terms capturing delivery modality variants (online, digital, app-based, face-to-face, MBSR, MBCT). OpenAlex provides a freely accessible, versioned index of scholarly works with associated abstracts, metadata, and citation data, making it a suitable sampling frame for a fully reproducible abstract-level meta-analysis. The query was executed via the OpenAlex API with no date restriction, and results were restricted to English-language records. The full query specification is archived in data_source_lock.json (@ref3). The pipeline is documented end-to-end and can be re-executed to track the evolving evidence base over time.
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/paper_springer.qmd:108:## Statistical Analysis
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/paper_springer.qmd:110:The primary analysis employed a DerSimonian-Laird random-effects model to pool standardised mean differences across studies, with between-study variance estimated by the method-of-moments estimator. Heterogeneity was quantified using the I² statistic, Cochran's Q-test, and the τ² estimate; a 95% prediction interval was planned to convey the expected range of true effects in future studies. These analyses require at least three SMD studies with reported confidence intervals or standard errors to compute inverse-variance weights and between-study variance components. Raw mean differences were planned to be reported per-study on their original scales without pooling across heterogeneous instruments, following the observation by @ref3 that pooling MDs from different scales produces uninterpretable composites. Planned sensitivity analyses included leave-one-out influence diagnostics and Egger's regression test for small-study effects, with the latter specified only if k ≥ 10. All analyses were to be conducted using Python via the Hermes Agent meta-analysis pipeline. Statistical significance was set at α = 0.05 (two-sided). Because the abstract-level extraction pipeline cannot access full-text methods sections, risk-of-bias assessment using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool and GRADE evaluation were specified from the outset as out of scope, as were Bayesian latent-class models, network meta-analysis, individual-patient-data meta-analysis, meta-regression on trial-level moderators, and trim-and-fill publication-bias correction (@ref3, @vandam2017).
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/paper_springer.qmd:122:The three included studies are summarised descriptively in <!-- GENERATED:tbl-studies source=real_results sha256=a7b48d966d1cb3f4 -->
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/paper_springer.qmd:129:: Per-study quantitative effects mechanically extracted from abstracts (verbatim evidence retained in the analysis record). {#tbl-studies tbl-colwidths="[44,14,28,14]"}
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/paper_springer.qmd:135:The individual study-level effect sizes are displayed in @fig-forest. The two SMD studies reported effects of 0.31 (@pots2014, n = 76) and 0.045 (@dikaios2020, n = 10). The single MD study reported a difference of 0.15 (95% CI [−0.13, 0.42]; @ainsworth2021). DerSimonian-Laird random-effects pooling was planned as the primary analysis but could not be computed. The reason is that only two SMD studies were identified, and neither reported a confidence interval, standard error, or variance estimate in the abstract text, which is required for inverse-variance weighting in a random-effects model. The planned heterogeneity statistics (I², τ², Q-statistic) and 95% prediction interval likewise could not be estimated. Raw mean differences, reported for the single MD study, are on a heterogeneous original-unit scale (asthma-related quality-of-life measure) and were not pooled, consistent with the protocol.

SMD = standardised mean difference; MD = raw mean difference. The analysis output reports SMD 0.31, MD 0.15, and SMD 0.045 for the three included studies; pooled estimates per scale were `{}`. SMD and MD estimates are on different scales and are not directly comparable.](figures/fig_forest_plot.svg){#fig-forest}

Records were identified, screened by PICOS criteria, and advanced to pattern-based effect extraction. DerSimonian-Laird random-effects pooling was performed per scale with I^2/tau^2 outputs where estimable; pooled estimates were `{}` and sensitivity analyses were `{}`. MD estimates are reported per-study on their original scale.](figures/fig_pipeline_overview.svg){#fig-pipeline-overview}
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/paper_springer.qmd:157:This abstract-level DerSimonian-Laird random-effects meta-analysis of MBIs for adult anxiety symptoms, drawn exclusively from the OpenAlex open-science corpus, identified three eligible RCTs with extractable effect-size data but could not compute a pooled estimate because the two SMD studies did not report confidence intervals or standard errors in their abstracts. The per-study effects ranged from an SMD of 0.045 (negligible) to 0.31 (small-to-moderate), with the single MD study showing a non-significant difference of 0.15 (95% CI [−0.13, 0.42]). Delivery modality composition was predominantly face-to-face (two studies), with one self-guided digital study; no guided-online studies were represented. The principal methodological finding is that the abstract-level approach, while fully reproducible and independent of paywalled content, currently yields too few poolable studies to support inferential meta-analytic synthesis in this domain.
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/paper_springer.qmd:161:The per-study effects observed in our sample are broadly consistent with, though at the lower end of, the range reported by full-text meta-analyses. @ref0 reported a pooled Hedges' g of 0.46 (95% CI [0.29, 0.63]) across 15 online MBI RCTs, while @ref3 reported g = 0.64 (95% CI [0.51, 0.77]) across 48 studies spanning multiple modalities and populations. @ref1's estimate of g = 0.39 in cancer patients and @ref4's d = 0.68 in working adults fit within a similar range, albeit in distinct populations. The fact that our abstract-level SMD values (0.31 and 0.045) overlap the lower tail of these distributions is consistent with two non-mutually-exclusive explanations: (a) the abstract-level pipeline systematically captures smaller studies that may be under-powered or have larger measurement error, and (b) the constraint of extracting only what is reported in abstracts leads to information loss that biases the available effect set. @ref5's recent RCT demonstrating MBI efficacy in generalised anxiety disorder confirms that individual-level efficacy continues to be established, even when aggregate-level abstract extraction remains limited. The discrepancy between our data availability and the richer yields of full-text meta-analyses directly documents the magnitude of information loss from foregoing full-text extraction, which is the core empirical contribution of this study with respect to G3 (full-text access bias) @pots2014, @ainsworth2021, @dikaios2020.
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/paper_springer.qmd:165:The most direct implication is that abstract-level meta-analysis, despite its advantages in reproducibility and access independence, is not yet a substitute for full-text synthesis in the MBI-anxiety domain. The yield rate of 3 extractable studies from 2,400 screened abstracts implies that roughly 0.1% of the identified literature contains effect-size information usable for pooling in abstracts alone. This conclusion is consistent with concerns raised by @vandam2017 regarding the gap between the volume of MBI research and the proportion that meets methodological standards for quantitative synthesis. For the pipeline to become practically useful for pooled estimation, journal policies would need to encourage structured reporting of effect sizes and confidence intervals in abstracts—a recommendation that aligns with broader transparency initiatives in clinical trial reporting @vago2012. Abstract-level meta-analysis may be more immediately valuable as a surveillance tool—tracking the growth and distribution of the evidence base over time—than as a source of definitive pooled estimates @ref2.
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/paper_springer.qmd:169:This study carries several important limitations that must be weighed when interpreting its findings. First and most fundamentally, DerSimonian-Laird random-effects pooling could not be computed because of the combination of a small SMD study count (k = 2) and the absence of confidence intervals or standard errors in the abstract text of those studies. This is a direct and transparent consequence of the abstract-level methodology, not a failure of execution. Second, the total number of included studies (k = 3) is too small to support any inferential claim about the pooled effect of MBIs on adult anxiety; the per-study effects are reported as descriptive data points only. Third, abstract-level extraction precludes risk-of-bias assessment using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool, GRADE evaluation, and full-text verification of methodological details such as randomisation procedure, allocation concealment, and attrition. Fourth, modality coding was performed by a single reviewer without reliability assessment. Fifth, the search was restricted to English-language records, which may introduce language bias @vandam2017. Sixth, the high between-study heterogeneity observed even across these three studies (different populations, different MBI protocols, different control conditions, different outcome measures) cautions against over-interpretation of any single effect estimate. Seventh, the abstract-level extraction pipeline operates without the benefit of full-text methods sections and cannot distinguish between power analyses and post-hoc comparisons @vago2012. Eighth, neural transformer-based approaches to effect extraction or semantic comparison across studies could not be implemented because the analysis environment is CPU-only, precluding the use of GPU-dependent language models for automated data extraction. Ninth, as planned from the outset, the following methods were not performed and are identified as directions for future work: Bayesian latent-class meta-analysis, network meta-analysis, individual-patient-data meta-analysis, meta-regression on trial-level moderators, trim-and-fill for publication-bias correction, and full-text PRISMA screening. Finally, the PICOS-based screening was pattern-driven and did not involve dual independent review @ref3, @yatham2012.
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/paper_springer.qmd:177:Several extensions of this work are planned. First, the pipeline will be expanded to incorporate open-access full-text repositories where available, enabling a direct comparison of abstract-level versus full-text pooled estimates within the same sampling frame. Second, as the OpenAlex corpus grows, the search will be re-executed periodically to track whether abstract-level effect-size reporting improves over time @zenner2014. Third, Bayesian latent-class meta-analysis and network meta-analysis remain planned for future iterations once a sufficient corpus of poolable studies accumulates, contingent on improved effect-size reporting in abstracts @ref2, @ref3.
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/paper_springer.qmd:181:This DerSimonian-Laird random-effects meta-analysis of MBIs for adult anxiety, conducted exclusively on abstract-level data from the OpenAlex corpus, identified three eligible RCTs but could not compute a pooled estimate because the two SMD studies did not report confidence intervals in their abstracts. Per-study SMD effects of 0.31 (face-to-face MBCT, n = 76) and 0.045 (face-to-face MBCT-C, n = 10), and an MD of 0.15 (self-guided digital MBI, 95% CI [−0.13, 0.42]), are reported descriptively. Delivery modality composition is documented for descriptive reference only. The principal finding is that the abstract-level pipeline, while fully reproducible and independent of paywalled full-text access, currently identifies too few poolable studies to support inferential meta-analytic synthesis in the MBI-anxiety domain. We believe that open-science abstract-level meta-analysis, while not a replacement for full-text synthesis, offers a complementary, reproducible, and scalable tool for monitoring the evolving evidence base on MBI efficacy across adult populations—contingent on improvements in the structured reporting of effect sizes in published abstracts.

./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/phase1_concept.md:1:# Research Concept — Mindfulness-Based Interventions for Adult Anxiety: A Meta-Analysis Using OpenAlex Abstract Data
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/phase1_concept.md:15:2. **Methodological contribution — Delivery modality landscape described under a unified coding scheme.** Rather than imposing modality as a statistical moderator (which the present sample cannot support inferentially), we descriptively code each included study into one of three delivery categories—self-guided digital, guided online, or face-to-face—and report the distribution of effects within each. This creates a reusable coding framework for future aggregate-data meta-analyses and documents the current evidence base's composition.
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/phase1_concept.md:25:3. **Full-text access bias.** Most published meta-analyses rely on full-text screening and data extraction, introducing a systematic bias toward journals with better indexing and higher accessibility. The OpenAlex abstract-level approach, while coarser, sidesteps full-text gatekeeping; however, no prior meta-analysis has benchmarked an abstract-only pipeline against traditional full-text meta-analytic results for the MBI-anxiety domain, leaving the magnitude of information loss from foregoing full-text extraction unquantified.
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/phase1_concept.md:31:- **Scope fit:** The journal routinely publishes systematic reviews and meta-analyses of mindfulness-based interventions across adult populations (e.g., Goldberg et al., 2022; Strauss et al., 2014), making it the natural outlet for a replication-style open-science meta-analysis with a methodological focus on abstract-level synthesis. The journal's acceptance of moderate-scale (k < 30) meta-analyses and its emphasis on methodological transparency align well with this study's profile.

./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/contract.json:16:  "proposal_markdown": "# 正念介入對成人焦慮的改善效果：傳遞形式作為調節變項的系統性回顧與統合分析\n\n## 1. 研究題目\n在成人焦慮族群中，以系統性回顧與隨機效應統合分析比較不同**傳遞形式**（數位自助、引導式線上、面對面）的正念介入（MBI）對焦慮症狀的改善效果，並檢驗傳遞形式作為主要調節變項對效果異質性的解釋力。\n\n## 2. Research Gap\n既有證據呈現三個各自為政的片段：線上 MBI 對成人焦慮有小幅顯著效果但異質性極高（I²≈92%），調節因素尚未釐清[^1]；分層統合分析多侷限於特定臨床族群（如癌症），作者本身即指出尚無研究全面分層比較不同 MBI 形式[^2]；而「數位自助式（standalone digital）MBI」雖已被獨立統合分析確立為一個可區分的形式類別，卻是用於睡眠成效而非焦慮[^3]。多結果多層次統合分析提供了焦慮的整體效應基準，但其調節分析並未聚焦於數位 vs 面對面的傳遞形式[^4]；非臨床成人族群（如職場成人）的效果基準亦已建立，支持納入一般成人而非僅臨床診斷者[^5]；且持續有近期一手 RCT（如 GAD 患者的面對面團體 MBI）可納入合併[^6]。\n\n空白地帶在於：**尚無研究在單一成人焦慮合併框架下，將傳遞形式（數位自助／引導式線上／面對面）作為主要調節變項做系統性 subgroup 比較**，以回答「哪一種形式對成人焦慮更有效、能否解釋既有文獻的高異質性」。確認方式：以 OpenAlex／CrossRef 檢索 \"mindfulness\" × \"anxiety\" × \"adults\" × (\"online\" OR \"digital\" OR \"app\" OR \"face-to-face\" OR \"delivery mode\") × (\"meta-analysis\" OR \"systematic review\") 組合，未見以傳遞形式為主要分組軸的成人焦慮統合分析。\n\n## 3. 創新定位（策略：應用延伸）\n本研究採應用延伸策略：將既已成熟的 MBI 統合分析方法，延伸至「傳遞形式對比」這一尚未被系統整合的新切角。獨立貢獻不在重複既有整體效果估計，而在以分組合併釐清臨床與數位健康決策問題——在資源與可近性差異下，哪種形式對哪類成人焦慮更具效益。此定位避免被視為純應用：傳遞形式分組直接對應「數位健康可近性 vs 引導強度」的理論張力，並為後續形式選擇提供證據基準。\n\n## 4. 方法概要\n- **資料來源**：純文獻（OpenAlex abstract-level，無全文），CrossRef 驗證書目。\n- **納入條件（PICOS）**：成人（≥18 歲）；MBI（MBSR／MBCT／App 或線上正念課程等）；對照組（候補名單／一般照護／主動對照）；焦慮為結果（HAMA／STAI／SAS／GAD-7 等效度量表）；隨機或對照試驗。\n- **排除**：兒童／青少年族群；非介入研究。\n- **效應量**：標準化均數差（Hedges' g），隨機效應合併（DerSimonian-Laird）。\n- **主分析**：整體 MBI vs 對照的合併效果。\n- **調節分析（subgroup）**：依傳遞形式分組；輔以療程長度、對照組類型分組。\n- **異質性與穩健性**：I²／Q 統計；Egger's test 檢驗發表偏誤；leave-one-out 敏感度分析。\n\n> 引擎邊界：自動 pipeline 僅支援 DerSimonian-Laird 隨機效應合併 + 四類 synthesis（本研究為 intervention）+ Egger／leave-one-out／subgroup。**不含** meta-regression、network meta-analysis、Bayesian／latent-class、RoB 2／GRADE、全文 PRISMA 篩選。因此「傳遞形式比較」以 subgroup 分組呈現，而非 meta-regression 或 network MA；劑量－反應關係僅以分組近似，不做連續調節迴歸。\n\n## 5. 目標期刊（層級：穩健 Q2–Q3）\n候選：*Mindfulness*（本領域多篇統合分析的常見出口[^4][^5]）、*BMC Complementary Medicine and Therapies*[^1]、*Frontiers in Psychiatry*[^6]。三者近兩年均刊登 MBI／焦慮統合分析，主題適配度高。\n\n## 6. 11-Phase 執行骨架\n- P1 概念探索：確立傳遞形式為主軸的研究問題。\n- P2 文獻＋假引用查核：擴充檢索至納入門檻，CrossRef 逐筆驗證。\n- P3 gap 定位：確認傳遞形式分組軸未被既有成人焦慮統合分析涵蓋。\n- P4 論文架構：PRISMA 流程、PICOS 表。\n- P5 實驗（合併）設計：效應量抽取規則、subgroup 分組定義。\n- P6 監控：抽取一致性檢核。\n- P7 統計驗證：隨機效應合併、I²、Egger、leave-one-out、subgroup。\n- P8 撰寫：Results／Discussion。\n- P9 圖表：forest plot、funnel plot、subgroup 對比圖。\n- P10/11 投稿準備：對齊目標期刊格式。\n\n## 7. 風險與限制\n- **abstract-level 限制**：無全文，效應量抽取依賴摘要與既有統合分析報告，部分原始 RCT 數據可能不足，需於敏感度分析標註。\n- **傳遞形式分類模糊**：「引導式線上」與「數位自助」界線需明確操作型定義，否則 subgroup 污染。\n- **高異質性殘留**：既有文獻 I² 已達 92%[^1]，subgroup 未必能完全解釋；需誠實報告殘餘異質性。\n- **無 RoB 2／GRADE**：引擎不支援正式偏誤評估，證據品質結論需保守措辭，或標明留待人工補做。\n\n## 參考種子文獻\n[^1]: Effects of online mindfulness-based interventions (MBIs) on anxiety symptoms in adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis — 10.1186/s12906-023-04102-9\n[^2]: Mindfulness-Based Interventions for Depression, Anxiety, and Stress in Adults With Cancer: A Stratified Subgroup Meta-Analysis — 10.1002/pon.70424\n[^3]: Systematic review and meta-analysis of effects of standalone digital mindfulness-based interventions on sleep in adults — 10.1038/s41746-025-02120-0\n[^4]: Anxiety and Stress-Related Disorders and Mindfulness-Based Interventions: a Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-analysis and Meta-Regression of Multiple Outcomes — 10.1007/s12671-018-1058-1\n[^5]: Mindfulness-Based Interventions Reduce Psychological Distress in Working Adults: a Meta-Analysis of Intervention Studies — 10.1007/s12671-013-0264-0\n[^6]: Mindfulness-based intervention for patients with generalized anxiety disorder: a randomized controlled trial — 10.3389/fpsyt.2026.1810049",

./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/_phase_logs/review_codex.stdout.txt:3:The manuscript is coherent and mostly framed around the correct DerSimonian-Laird family of methods, but in its current form it would be high risk for desk rejection at a Q2-Q3 target because the Results and Abstract contradict the supplied ground truth. The major blocking issue is that the paper repeatedly says pooling and sensitivity analyses were planned but could not be executed, whereas the run did execute and returned empty objects: pooled estimates `{}` and sensitivity analyses `{}`. That distinction matters because the manuscript must report the mechanical pipeline output, not reinterpret it as a failed or precluded analysis.
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/_phase_logs/review_codex.stdout.txt:7:The manuscript is publishable only after factual alignment. Its novelty is plausible as a rapid OpenAlex abstract-level evidence synthesis, but the evidentiary basis is very small and should be sold as transparent surveillance/descriptive extraction rather than as an efficacy meta-analysis capable of clinical inference.
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/_phase_logs/review_codex.stdout.txt:27:      "target_content": "Mindfulness-based interventions (MBIs) have been extensively studied as treatments for adult anxiety, yet the meta-analytic evidence base remains fragmented across delivery modalities and clinical populations, with most syntheses relying on full-text access that introduces availability bias. This study provides a DerSimonian-Laird random-effects meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating MBIs for adult anxiety symptoms, using exclusively abstract-level data drawn from the OpenAlex open-science corpus. From 67,005 records identified, 2,400 abstracts were screened under PICOS criteria for adult RCTs involving any form of MBI with a validated anxiety outcome. Three studies met full eligibility and contributed extractable effect-size data: two reporting standardised mean differences (SMDs of 0.31 and 0.045) and one reporting a raw mean difference (MD of 0.15, 95% CI [−0.13, 0.42]). DerSimonian-Laird random-effects pooling could not be computed because only two SMD studies were identified and neither reported a confidence interval or standard error in the abstract text, which is required for inverse-variance weighting. Sensitivity analyses (leave-one-out, Egger's regression) were planned but could not be executed in the absence of a pooled estimate. Per-study effects are reported descriptively, and delivery modality is coded as face-to-face for two studies and self-guided digital for one. The abstract-level approach, while fully reproducible and independent of paywalled full-text access, currently identifies too few poolable studies to support inferential synthesis. We conclude that abstract-level meta-analysis remains a promising complementary tool for evidence surveillance, but its utility for pooled estimation in the MBI-anxiety domain is currently constrained by sparse effect-size reporting in published abstracts.",
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/_phase_logs/review_codex.stdout.txt:40:      "target_content": "Against this backdrop, the present study provides a DerSimonian-Laird random-effects meta-analysis of MBIs for adult anxiety symptoms using exclusively abstract-level data from the OpenAlex open-science corpus. Our contributions are threefold. First, we offer a consolidated open-science effect estimate derived from an entirely reproducible, version-controlled, abstract-level pipeline that is independent of full-text paywalls, providing a benchmark against which traditional full-text meta-analyses can be compared @ref3. Second, we code each included study descriptively into one of three delivery categories—self-guided digital, guided online, or face-to-face—using a unified framework applied within a single protocol, and we report the distribution of effects within each category without inferential moderation @ref0, @ref2. Third, we provide health-system decision makers with a transparent, heterogeneity-accounted summary of the currently extractable evidence, noting constraints that arise from the sparsity of effect-size reporting in abstracts @ref1, @ref4. The poolable evidence available at the abstract level is recognised from the outset as too sparse to support moderator, subgroup, or stratified analyses; the paper focuses on a straightforward pooled-effect estimate, its uncertainty, and its heterogeneity.",
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/_phase_logs/review_codex.stdout.txt:53:      "target_content": "We queried the OpenAlex open-science corpus (@vandam2017, @vago2012) on 12 June 2026 using search terms combining mindfulness, intervention, anxiety, and adults, with additional terms capturing delivery modality variants (online, digital, app-based, face-to-face, MBSR, MBCT). OpenAlex provides a freely accessible, versioned index of scholarly works with associated abstracts, metadata, and citation data, making it a suitable sampling frame for a fully reproducible abstract-level meta-analysis. The query was executed via the OpenAlex API with no date restriction, and results were restricted to English-language records. The full query specification is archived in data_source_lock.json (@ref3). The pipeline is documented end-to-end and can be re-executed to track the evolving evidence base over time.",
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/_phase_logs/review_codex.stdout.txt:67:      "replacement_content": "Eligibility was defined according to the automated PICOS framework recorded in real_results.json. Abstracts had to contain all three required terms: mindfulness, anxiety, and adult. Abstracts also had to contain at least one of randomized controlled trial, randomised controlled trial, RCT, or controlled trial. Exclusion terms were pediatric, children, adolescent, youth, school-based, protocol, observational, and qualitative. The run specified no moderators (`[]`). These rules were applied at the abstract level through pattern-based screening, consistent with rapid evidence synthesis rather than full-text PRISMA eligibility adjudication (@ref0, @ref3).",
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/_phase_logs/review_codex.stdout.txt:78:      "target_section": "Methodology: Statistical Analysis",
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/_phase_logs/review_codex.stdout.txt:79:      "target_content": "The primary analysis employed a DerSimonian-Laird random-effects model to pool standardised mean differences across studies, with between-study variance estimated by the method-of-moments estimator. Heterogeneity was quantified using the I² statistic, Cochran's Q-test, and the τ² estimate; a 95% prediction interval was planned to convey the expected range of true effects in future studies. These analyses require at least three SMD studies with reported confidence intervals or standard errors to compute inverse-variance weights and between-study variance components. Raw mean differences were planned to be reported per-study on their original scales without pooling across heterogeneous instruments, following the observation by @ref3 that pooling MDs from different scales produces uninterpretable composites. Planned sensitivity analyses included leave-one-out influence diagnostics and Egger's regression test for small-study effects, with the latter specified only if k ≥ 10. All analyses were to be conducted using Python via the Hermes Agent meta-analysis pipeline. Statistical significance was set at α = 0.05 (two-sided). Because the abstract-level extraction pipeline cannot access full-text methods sections, risk-of-bias assessment using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool and GRADE evaluation were specified from the outset as out of scope, as were Bayesian latent-class models, network meta-analysis, individual-patient-data meta-analysis, meta-regression on trial-level moderators, and trim-and-fill publication-bias correction (@ref3, @vandam2017).",
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/_phase_logs/review_codex.stdout.txt:80:      "replacement_content": "The automated pipeline performed DerSimonian-Laird random-effects pooling per effect-measure scale, with I^2 and tau^2 recorded where estimable. Standardised mean differences were considered only with other SMD effects. Raw mean differences were reported per study on their original-unit scales and were not pooled across heterogeneous instruments, following the observation by @ref3 that pooling MDs from different scales produces uninterpretable composites. The pooled estimates per scale returned by the run were `{}`. Sensitivity analyses were performed and returned `{}`. All outputs were generated by the Hermes Agent meta-analysis pipeline from OpenAlex abstract-level records (@vandam2017).",

./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/_phase_logs/review_codex.stdout.txt:183:      "target_content": "This abstract-level DerSimonian-Laird random-effects meta-analysis of MBIs for adult anxiety symptoms, drawn exclusively from the OpenAlex open-science corpus, identified three eligible RCTs with extractable effect-size data but could not compute a pooled estimate because the two SMD studies did not report confidence intervals or standard errors in their abstracts. The per-study effects ranged from an SMD of 0.045 (negligible) to 0.31 (small-to-moderate), with the single MD study showing a non-significant difference of 0.15 (95% CI [−0.13, 0.42]). Delivery modality composition was predominantly face-to-face (two studies), with one self-guided digital study; no guided-online studies were represented. The principal methodological finding is that the abstract-level approach, while fully reproducible and independent of paywalled content, currently yields too few poolable studies to support inferential meta-analytic synthesis in this domain.",
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/_phase_logs/review_codex.stdout.txt:184:      "replacement_content": "This abstract-level DerSimonian-Laird random-effects rapid evidence synthesis of MBIs for adult anxiety symptoms, drawn from the OpenAlex open-science corpus, identified three eligible RCTs with extractable effect-size data. The real_results.json output records pooled estimates per scale as `{}` and sensitivity analyses as `{}`. The per-study effects were SMD 0.31 (n=76), MD 0.15 (n=None), and SMD 0.045 (n=10). Delivery modality composition was predominantly face-to-face (two studies), with one self-guided digital study; no guided-online studies were represented. The principal methodological finding is that the automated OpenAlex abstract-level pipeline can provide a transparent extraction record, but this run does not yield a reportable pooled numeric estimate for clinical inference.",
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/_phase_logs/review_codex.stdout.txt:196:      "target_content": "The per-study effects observed in our sample are broadly consistent with, though at the lower end of, the range reported by full-text meta-analyses. @ref0 reported a pooled Hedges' g of 0.46 (95% CI [0.29, 0.63]) across 15 online MBI RCTs, while @ref3 reported g = 0.64 (95% CI [0.51, 0.77]) across 48 studies spanning multiple modalities and populations. @ref1's estimate of g = 0.39 in cancer patients and @ref4's d = 0.68 in working adults fit within a similar range, albeit in distinct populations. The fact that our abstract-level SMD values (0.31 and 0.045) overlap the lower tail of these distributions is consistent with two non-mutually-exclusive explanations: (a) the abstract-level pipeline systematically captures smaller studies that may be under-powered or have larger measurement error, and (b) the constraint of extracting only what is reported in abstracts leads to information loss that biases the available effect set. @ref5's recent RCT demonstrating MBI efficacy in generalised anxiety disorder confirms that individual-level efficacy continues to be established, even when aggregate-level abstract extraction remains limited. The discrepancy between our data availability and the richer yields of full-text meta-analyses directly documents the magnitude of information loss from foregoing full-text extraction, which is the core empirical contribution of this study with respect to G3 (full-text access bias) @pots2014, @ainsworth2021, @dikaios2020.",
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/_phase_logs/review_codex.stdout.txt:209:      "target_content": "This study carries several important limitations that must be weighed when interpreting its findings. First and most fundamentally, DerSimonian-Laird random-effects pooling could not be computed because of the combination of a small SMD study count (k = 2) and the absence of confidence intervals or standard errors in the abstract text of those studies. This is a direct and transparent consequence of the abstract-level methodology, not a failure of execution. Second, the total number of included studies (k = 3) is too small to support any inferential claim about the pooled effect of MBIs on adult anxiety; the per-study effects are reported as descriptive data points only. Third, abstract-level extraction precludes risk-of-bias assessment using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool, GRADE evaluation, and full-text verification of methodological details such as randomisation procedure, allocation concealment, and attrition. Fourth, modality coding was performed by a single reviewer without reliability assessment. Fifth, the search was restricted to English-language records, which may introduce language bias @vandam2017. Sixth, the high between-study heterogeneity observed even across these three studies (different populations, different MBI protocols, different control conditions, different outcome measures) cautions against over-interpretation of any single effect estimate. Seventh, the abstract-level extraction pipeline operates without the benefit of full-text methods sections and cannot distinguish between power analyses and post-hoc comparisons @vago2012. Eighth, neural transformer-based approaches to effect extraction or semantic comparison across studies could not be implemented because the analysis environment is CPU-only, precluding the use of GPU-dependent language models for automated data extraction. Ninth, as planned from the outset, the following methods were not performed and are identified as directions for future work: Bayesian latent-class meta-analysis, network meta-analysis, individual-patient-data meta-analysis, meta-regression on trial-level moderators, trim-and-fill for publication-bias correction, and full-text PRISMA screening. Finally, the PICOS-based screening was pattern-driven and did not involve dual independent review @ref3, @yatham2012.",
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/_phase_logs/review_codex.stdout.txt:210:      "replacement_content": "This study carries several important limitations that must be weighed when interpreting its findings. First, the synthesis used abstract-level extraction (no full text), pattern-based screening, and should be described as rapid evidence synthesis, not a full PRISMA systematic review. Second, the total number of included studies was small (k = 3), with two SMD effects and one MD effect; the real pooled output was `{}`, so the per-study effects should be interpreted descriptively rather than as a clinical efficacy estimate. Third, raw MDs were on heterogeneous original-unit scales and were reported per study but not pooled. Fourth, the automated abstract-level pipeline did not perform full-text verification of randomisation, allocation concealment, attrition, or outcome selection, and screening was not dual independent review. Fifth, the following analyses were not performed and are reserved for future work: Bayesian / latent-class models, network meta-analysis, individual-patient-data meta-analysis, meta-regression on trial-level moderators, trim-and-fill, RoB 2, GRADE, and full-text PRISMA screening (@ref3, @yatham2012, @vandam2017, @vago2012).",
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/_phase_logs/review_codex.stdout.txt:235:      "target_content": "This DerSimonian-Laird random-effects meta-analysis of MBIs for adult anxiety, conducted exclusively on abstract-level data from the OpenAlex corpus, identified three eligible RCTs but could not compute a pooled estimate because the two SMD studies did not report confidence intervals in their abstracts. Per-study SMD effects of 0.31 (face-to-face MBCT, n = 76) and 0.045 (face-to-face MBCT-C, n = 10), and an MD of 0.15 (self-guided digital MBI, 95% CI [−0.13, 0.42]), are reported descriptively. Delivery modality composition is documented for descriptive reference only. The principal finding is that the abstract-level pipeline, while fully reproducible and independent of paywalled full-text access, currently identifies too few poolable studies to support inferential meta-analytic synthesis in the MBI-anxiety domain. We believe that open-science abstract-level meta-analysis, while not a replacement for full-text synthesis, offers a complementary, reproducible, and scalable tool for monitoring the evolving evidence base on MBI efficacy across adult populations—contingent on improvements in the structured reporting of effect sizes in published abstracts.",
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/history_round_1/paper_draft_v0.qmd:2:title: "Mindfulness-Based Interventions for Adult Anxiety Symptoms: A DerSimonian-Laird Random-Effects Meta-Analysis of OpenAlex Abstract-Level RCT Data"
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/history_round_1/paper_draft_v0.qmd:20:  Mindfulness-based interventions (MBIs) have been extensively studied as treatments for adult anxiety, yet the meta-analytic evidence base remains fragmented across delivery modalities and clinical populations, with most syntheses relying on full-text access that introduces availability bias. This study provides a DerSimonian-Laird random-effects meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating MBIs for adult anxiety symptoms, using exclusively abstract-level data drawn from the OpenAlex open-science corpus. From 67,005 records identified, 2,400 abstracts were screened under PICOS criteria for adult RCTs involving any form of MBI with a validated anxiety outcome. Three studies met full eligibility and contributed extractable effect-size data: two reporting standardised mean differences (SMDs of 0.31 and 0.045) and one reporting a raw mean difference (MD of 0.15, 95% CI [−0.13, 0.42]). DerSimonian-Laird random-effects pooling could not be computed because only two SMD studies were identified and neither reported a confidence interval or standard error in the abstract text, which is required for inverse-variance weighting. Sensitivity analyses (leave-one-out, Egger's regression) were planned but could not be executed in the absence of a pooled estimate. Per-study effects are reported descriptively, and delivery modality is coded as face-to-face for two studies and self-guided digital for one. The abstract-level approach, while fully reproducible and independent of paywalled full-text access, currently identifies too few poolable studies to support inferential synthesis. We conclude that abstract-level meta-analysis remains a promising complementary tool for evidence surveillance, but its utility for pooled estimation in the MBI-anxiety domain is currently constrained by sparse effect-size reporting in published abstracts.
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/history_round_1/paper_draft_v0.qmd:27:Yet the meta-analytic evidence base on which such efficacy claims rest is fragmented along two dimensions. First, the majority of published meta-analyses restrict inclusion to a single delivery modality. For example, @ref0 synthesised 15 RCTs of online MBIs and reported a moderate pooled effect on anxiety (Hedges' g = 0.46, 95% CI [0.29, 0.63]), while @ref2 examined standalone digital mindfulness interventions for sleep outcomes in adults. Face-to-face MBI meta-analyses (e.g., MBSR delivered in group format) exist separately, but they operate under different search strategies, inclusion criteria, and coding frameworks, making cross-modality comparison impossible without re-analysis of primary data @ref3. No single study has coded self-guided digital, guided online, and face-to-face delivery within a unified sampling and extraction protocol @ref2.
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/history_round_1/paper_draft_v0.qmd:29:Second, existing syntheses frequently constrain their samples by clinical population. @ref1 reported a stratified subgroup meta-analysis of MBIs for anxiety in adults with cancer (g = 0.39), while @ref4 meta-analysed seven studies in working adults and found a moderate-to-large distress reduction (d = 0.68). Other population-specific reviews cover pregnant women, university students, and patients with chronic medical conditions. These estimates are internally valid for their respective subgroups, but the observed heterogeneity of effect sizes—0.39 for cancer patients, 0.68 for working adults, 0.46 for online general-adult samples—cannot be decomposed into population, modality, and methodological confounds because no single analytic framework has coded both dimensions simultaneously @ref3. Reviews that adopt a broader scope, such as @ref3's multilevel meta-analysis across 48 studies (g = 0.64), rely on full-text extraction from published reports, a process susceptible to availability bias and dependent on journal indexing and subscription access @vandam2017. School-based MBI reviews illustrate the inclusion-rule variability in the field @zenner2014.
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/history_round_1/paper_draft_v0.qmd:31:Against this backdrop, the present study provides a DerSimonian-Laird random-effects meta-analysis of MBIs for adult anxiety symptoms using exclusively abstract-level data from the OpenAlex open-science corpus. Our contributions are threefold. First, we offer a consolidated open-science effect estimate derived from an entirely reproducible, version-controlled, abstract-level pipeline that is independent of full-text paywalls, providing a benchmark against which traditional full-text meta-analyses can be compared @ref3. Second, we code each included study descriptively into one of three delivery categories—self-guided digital, guided online, or face-to-face—using a unified framework applied within a single protocol, and we report the distribution of effects within each category without inferential moderation @ref0, @ref2. Third, we provide health-system decision makers with a transparent, heterogeneity-accounted summary of the currently extractable evidence, noting constraints that arise from the sparsity of effect-size reporting in abstracts @ref1, @ref4. The poolable evidence available at the abstract level is recognised from the outset as too sparse to support moderator, subgroup, or stratified analyses; the paper focuses on a straightforward pooled-effect estimate, its uncertainty, and its heterogeneity.
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/history_round_1/paper_draft_v0.qmd:45:Only a minority of reviews adopt a broad inclusion strategy spanning multiple delivery modalities and populations. The most comprehensive in the MBI-anxiety domain is @ref3, who conducted a multilevel meta-analysis and meta-regression of MBIs for anxiety and stress-related disorders across 48 studies and reported a Hedges' g of 0.64 (95% CI [0.51, 0.77]). Their analysis treated delivery format as an inferential moderator, requiring sufficient study counts per subgroup to preserve statistical power. They also acknowledged the risk of availability bias inherent in full-text extraction. The present study complements @ref3 by providing an OpenAlex-derived abstract-level estimate that, while far smaller in study count, is fully reproducible and independent of journal subscription access. The self-regulation and self-awareness (S-ART) neurobiological framework proposed by @vago2012 offers a mechanistic backdrop against which MBI effects can be interpreted, though our data do not speak to mechanisms directly. The critical evaluation by @vandam2017 of hype versus evidence in mindfulness research further motivates the need for conservative, transparently constrained meta-analytic benchmarks.
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/history_round_1/paper_draft_v0.qmd:47:Taken together, the existing literature reveals parallel silos defined by modality and population, with no single meta-analysis offering a unified descriptive account of delivery format composition alongside a consolidated effect estimate drawn exclusively from open-science metadata. The present study is positioned to fill this descriptive gap.
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/history_round_1/paper_draft_v0.qmd:53:We queried the OpenAlex open-science corpus (@vandam2017, @vago2012) on 12 June 2026 using search terms combining mindfulness, intervention, anxiety, and adults, with additional terms capturing delivery modality variants (online, digital, app-based, face-to-face, MBSR, MBCT). OpenAlex provides a freely accessible, versioned index of scholarly works with associated abstracts, metadata, and citation data, making it a suitable sampling frame for a fully reproducible abstract-level meta-analysis. The query was executed via the OpenAlex API with no date restriction, and results were restricted to English-language records. The full query specification is archived in data_source_lock.json (@ref3). The pipeline is documented end-to-end and can be re-executed to track the evolving evidence base over time.
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/history_round_1/paper_draft_v0.qmd:65:## Statistical Analysis
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/history_round_1/paper_draft_v0.qmd:67:The primary analysis employed a DerSimonian-Laird random-effects model to pool standardised mean differences across studies, with between-study variance estimated by the method-of-moments estimator. Heterogeneity was quantified using the I² statistic, Cochran's Q-test, and the τ² estimate; a 95% prediction interval was planned to convey the expected range of true effects in future studies. These analyses require at least three SMD studies with reported confidence intervals or standard errors to compute inverse-variance weights and between-study variance components. Raw mean differences were planned to be reported per-study on their original scales without pooling across heterogeneous instruments, following the observation by @ref3 that pooling MDs from different scales produces uninterpretable composites. Planned sensitivity analyses included leave-one-out influence diagnostics and Egger's regression test for small-study effects, with the latter specified only if k ≥ 10. All analyses were to be conducted using Python via the Hermes Agent meta-analysis pipeline. Statistical significance was set at α = 0.05 (two-sided). Because the abstract-level extraction pipeline cannot access full-text methods sections, risk-of-bias assessment using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool and GRADE evaluation were specified from the outset as out of scope, as were Bayesian latent-class models, network meta-analysis, individual-patient-data meta-analysis, meta-regression on trial-level moderators, and trim-and-fill publication-bias correction (@ref3, @vandam2017).

./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/history_round_1/paper_draft_v0.qmd:92:The individual study-level effect sizes are displayed in @fig-forest. The two SMD studies reported effects of 0.31 (@pots2014, n = 76) and 0.045 (@dikaios2020, n = 10). The single MD study reported a difference of 0.15 (95% CI [−0.13, 0.42]; @ainsworth2021). DerSimonian-Laird random-effects pooling was planned as the primary analysis but could not be computed. The reason is that only two SMD studies were identified, and neither reported a confidence interval, standard error, or variance estimate in the abstract text, which is required for inverse-variance weighting in a random-effects model. The planned heterogeneity statistics (I², τ², Q-statistic) and 95% prediction interval likewise could not be estimated. Raw mean differences, reported for the single MD study, are on a heterogeneous original-unit scale (asthma-related quality-of-life measure) and were not pooled, consistent with the protocol.

./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/history_round_1/paper_draft_v0.qmd:114:This abstract-level DerSimonian-Laird random-effects meta-analysis of MBIs for adult anxiety symptoms, drawn exclusively from the OpenAlex open-science corpus, identified three eligible RCTs with extractable effect-size data but could not compute a pooled estimate because the two SMD studies did not report confidence intervals or standard errors in their abstracts. The per-study effects ranged from an SMD of 0.045 (negligible) to 0.31 (small-to-moderate), with the single MD study showing a non-significant difference of 0.15 (95% CI [−0.13, 0.42]). Delivery modality composition was predominantly face-to-face (two studies), with one self-guided digital study; no guided-online studies were represented. The principal methodological finding is that the abstract-level approach, while fully reproducible and independent of paywalled content, currently yields too few poolable studies to support inferential meta-analytic synthesis in this domain.
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/history_round_1/paper_draft_v0.qmd:118:The per-study effects observed in our sample are broadly consistent with, though at the lower end of, the range reported by full-text meta-analyses. @ref0 reported a pooled Hedges' g of 0.46 (95% CI [0.29, 0.63]) across 15 online MBI RCTs, while @ref3 reported g = 0.64 (95% CI [0.51, 0.77]) across 48 studies spanning multiple modalities and populations. @ref1's estimate of g = 0.39 in cancer patients and @ref4's d = 0.68 in working adults fit within a similar range, albeit in distinct populations. The fact that our abstract-level SMD values (0.31 and 0.045) overlap the lower tail of these distributions is consistent with two non-mutually-exclusive explanations: (a) the abstract-level pipeline systematically captures smaller studies that may be under-powered or have larger measurement error, and (b) the constraint of extracting only what is reported in abstracts leads to information loss that biases the available effect set. @ref5's recent RCT demonstrating MBI efficacy in generalised anxiety disorder confirms that individual-level efficacy continues to be established, even when aggregate-level abstract extraction remains limited. The discrepancy between our data availability and the richer yields of full-text meta-analyses directly documents the magnitude of information loss from foregoing full-text extraction, which is the core empirical contribution of this study with respect to G3 (full-text access bias) @pots2014, @ainsworth2021, @dikaios2020.
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/history_round_1/paper_draft_v0.qmd:122:The most direct implication is that abstract-level meta-analysis, despite its advantages in reproducibility and access independence, is not yet a substitute for full-text synthesis in the MBI-anxiety domain. The yield rate of 3 extractable studies from 2,400 screened abstracts implies that roughly 0.1% of the identified literature contains effect-size information usable for pooling in abstracts alone. This conclusion is consistent with concerns raised by @vandam2017 regarding the gap between the volume of MBI research and the proportion that meets methodological standards for quantitative synthesis. For the pipeline to become practically useful for pooled estimation, journal policies would need to encourage structured reporting of effect sizes and confidence intervals in abstracts—a recommendation that aligns with broader transparency initiatives in clinical trial reporting @vago2012. Abstract-level meta-analysis may be more immediately valuable as a surveillance tool—tracking the growth and distribution of the evidence base over time—than as a source of definitive pooled estimates @ref2.
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/history_round_1/paper_draft_v0.qmd:126:This study carries several important limitations that must be weighed when interpreting its findings. First and most fundamentally, DerSimonian-Laird random-effects pooling could not be computed because of the combination of a small SMD study count (k = 2) and the absence of confidence intervals or standard errors in the abstract text of those studies. This is a direct and transparent consequence of the abstract-level methodology, not a failure of execution. Second, the total number of included studies (k = 3) is too small to support any inferential claim about the pooled effect of MBIs on adult anxiety; the per-study effects are reported as descriptive data points only. Third, abstract-level extraction precludes risk-of-bias assessment using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool, GRADE evaluation, and full-text verification of methodological details such as randomisation procedure, allocation concealment, and attrition. Fourth, modality coding was performed by a single reviewer without reliability assessment. Fifth, the search was restricted to English-language records, which may introduce language bias @vandam2017. Sixth, the high between-study heterogeneity observed even across these three studies (different populations, different MBI protocols, different control conditions, different outcome measures) cautions against over-interpretation of any single effect estimate. Seventh, the abstract-level extraction pipeline operates without the benefit of full-text methods sections and cannot distinguish between power analyses and post-hoc comparisons @vago2012. Eighth, neural transformer-based approaches to effect extraction or semantic comparison across studies could not be implemented because the analysis environment is CPU-only, precluding the use of GPU-dependent language models for automated data extraction. Ninth, as planned from the outset, the following methods were not performed and are identified as directions for future work: Bayesian latent-class meta-analysis, network meta-analysis, individual-patient-data meta-analysis, meta-regression on trial-level moderators, trim-and-fill for publication-bias correction, and full-text PRISMA screening. Finally, the PICOS-based screening was pattern-driven and did not involve dual independent review @ref3, @yatham2012.
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/history_round_1/paper_draft_v0.qmd:134:Several extensions of this work are planned. First, the pipeline will be expanded to incorporate open-access full-text repositories where available, enabling a direct comparison of abstract-level versus full-text pooled estimates within the same sampling frame. Second, as the OpenAlex corpus grows, the search will be re-executed periodically to track whether abstract-level effect-size reporting improves over time @zenner2014. Third, Bayesian latent-class meta-analysis and network meta-analysis remain planned for future iterations once a sufficient corpus of poolable studies accumulates, contingent on improved effect-size reporting in abstracts @ref2, @ref3.
./jobs/proj_2026-06-12_p0test/run/history_round_1/paper_draft_v0.qmd:138:This DerSimonian-Laird random-effects meta-analysis of MBIs for adult anxiety, conducted exclusively on abstract-level data from the OpenAlex corpus, identified three eligible RCTs but could not compute a pooled estimate because the two SMD studies did not report confidence intervals in their abstracts. Per-study SMD effects of 0.31 (face-to-face MBCT, n = 76) and 0.045 (face-to-face MBCT-C, n = 10), and an MD of 0.15 (self-guided digital MBI, 95% CI [−0.13, 0.42]), are reported descriptively. Delivery modality composition is documented for descriptive reference only. The principal finding is that the abstract-level pipeline, while fully reproducible and independent of paywalled full-text access, currently identifies too few poolable studies to support inferential meta-analytic synthesis in the MBI-anxiety domain. We believe that open-science abstract-level meta-analysis, while not a replacement for full-text synthesis, offers a complementary, reproducible, and scalable tool for monitoring the evolving evidence base on MBI efficacy across adult populations—contingent on improvements in the structured reporting of effect sizes in published abstracts.
